title: Letting Go of Control
author: Pursuing Pragmatic Leadership
summary: The author's 10-year-old son's confrontation -- 'You expect me to be like you, and I can't' -- opens a penetrating examination of the difference between control and responsibility in leadership. Control attempts to manage others' outcomes and decisions; responsibility means owning your own actions and inputs. Control creates dependency through what the author calls 'pattern inversion': the space leaders occupy is the space their team learns to vacate. The author traces his own controlling patterns to childhood adaptive responses to instability, and names four subtle ways control masquerades as responsibility: stepping in to fix problems instead of coaching, refusing to delegate because no one else will approach work with sufficient rigor, setting standards that actually mean 'our way,' and intervening when watching others struggle becomes personally uncomfortable. Letting go does not mean lower standards, hands-off management, or avoiding accountability -- it means releasing attachment to one specific execution path and trusting the process. The paradox: when leaders loosen their grip, their actual influence tends to increase because people step into genuine ownership, develop problem-solving capability, and bring their own strengths rather than replicating the leader's.
points: * Control focuses on outcomes leaders cannot fully dictate; responsibility focuses on the inputs they can directly influence through their own behavior -- the critical distinction is that control manages what others do while responsibility manages what we do. * Pattern inversion: the space a leader occupies is the space their team learns to vacate -- when leaders consistently manage the chaos, the people around them stop developing the capability to handle it themselves. * Four subtle forms of control masquerading as responsibility: stepping in to fix problems instead of coaching, refusing to delegate, setting standards that mean 'our way,' and intervening when watching others struggle becomes personally uncomfortable. * Letting go means releasing attachment to having things happen in one specific way -- trusting that others can reach similar outcomes via different paths, becoming comfortable with uncertainty, and accepting that mistakes are part of developing resilience and capability. * The paradox of control: when leaders stop trying to manage every detail, people step up with more ownership, develop their own problem-solving capability, and bring strengths the leader couldn't have accessed alone -- actual influence grows.
quotes: You expect me to be like you, and I can't.
The critical difference is that control attempts to manage what other people do, while responsibility focuses on managing what we do ourselves.
There's a principle I've written about before called pattern inversion. The space we occupy as leaders is the space our team learns to vacate.
He was saying he felt like he couldn't be himself around me.
Letting go of control isn't the same as abandoning responsibility or lowering our standards.
There's something paradoxical here. When we stop trying to control every detail, our actual influence tends to increase.
